prompt: Why does the lesson compare two servers by querying `pg_settings` instead of diffing their configuration files?
hint: Count the places a value can come from.

choices.text: The configuration files are unreadable without sudo, so a query is the only way an ordinary user can see them
choices.why: postgresql.conf is readable by anybody on Ubuntu; the lesson ran wc on it as ana. Permissions are not the reason.

choices.text: diff cannot compare files that live on two different machines
choices.why: Copying one file across is trivial. The problem is what the files leave out, not where they are.

choices.text: pg_settings is faster to read than a file of eight hundred lines
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; a diff of eight hundred lines takes no time at all.

choices.text: Files are one source among several
choices.why: Right. postgresql.auto.conf and settings kept in the catalogue never show up in a diff of /etc, and the running server knows the result of all of them.

prompt: In the lesson's diff, main had `lc_messages = C.UTF-8` and staging had `lc_messages = C`. Where did that difference come from?
hint: Nobody typed a locale anywhere.

choices.text: Somebody ran ALTER SYSTEM on staging
choices.why: Nothing was ever run on staging. An ALTER SYSTEM would also have shown postgresql.auto.conf as the source.

choices.text: The environment each cluster was created in
choices.why: Right. pg_createcluster takes the locale from the environment of the command that runs it, and the installer and sudo from a shell had different ones.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 uses C for every cluster after the first one on a machine
choices.why: There is no such rule; a second cluster made from a UTF-8 environment gets a UTF-8 locale.

choices.text: The staging cluster's port, 5433, selects a different locale table
choices.why: A port decides where clients connect, and nothing about language or sorting.

prompt: `ALTER DATABASE shop SET random_page_cost = 1.1` was run on main, yet the diff of `settings.sql` output did not show it. Why?
hint: Which database did `psql -f settings.sql` connect to?

choices.text: It needs a restart before pg_settings shows it
choices.why: random_page_cost needs no restart. The setting was in force, just not for the database the query ran in.

choices.text: The query excludes the source 'database'
choices.why: settings.sql excludes default, override and client only. A per-database value would have appeared had the query run inside shop.

choices.text: ALTER DATABASE writes to postgresql.auto.conf, which the diff ignored
choices.why: ALTER DATABASE writes to the catalogue, not to any file. The diff did show the postgresql.auto.conf value, work_mem.

choices.text: The query ran in the database ana
choices.why: Right. A setting attached to shop applies only to connections to shop; \drds lists it from anywhere.

prompt: The psql command that lists settings attached to databases and roles, which no configuration file holds, is \___.
hint: d, then the initials of role, database, settings.

prompt: Why does the lesson put the shop's settings in conf.d/50-shop.conf rather than editing postgresql.conf?
hint: Think of the file the next major version generates.

choices.text: PostgreSQL ignores edits to postgresql.conf on Ubuntu
choices.why: It reads them like any other line. The trouble is finding and carrying them, not whether they work.

choices.text: Files in conf.d are read before postgresql.conf, so they set the defaults
choices.why: They are read after it, which is why a value in them wins over the main file.

choices.text: A changed line is lost among eight hundred
choices.why: Right. A small file of your own can be compared, reviewed and copied whole; an edit inside a generated template cannot.

choices.text: postgresql.conf belongs to the postgres user and cannot be committed to git
choices.why: Ownership has nothing to do with git; any file can be copied into a repository.

prompt: conf.d holds `20-logging.conf` with `log_min_duration_statement = 1s` and `90-local.conf` with `log_min_duration_statement = 250ms`. postgresql.auto.conf is empty. What does the server run with?
hint: Name order, and the later one wins.

choices.text: 250ms
choices.why: Right. 90-local.conf sorts after 20-logging.conf, so its line is read later and wins.

choices.text: 1s, because the lower number has priority
choices.why: The number only sets the reading order, and a later value replaces an earlier one.

choices.text: Neither: the server refuses a parameter set in two files
choices.why: Setting a parameter twice is allowed; pg_file_settings marks the earlier one as not applied.

choices.text: Whichever file was modified most recently
choices.why: Modification times play no part; the order is the order of the names.

prompt: At 3 a.m. somebody runs `ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '128MB'` and goes back to bed. Next week the repository's 50-shop.conf is changed to `work_mem = 32MB` and deployed. What does the server run with, and why?
hint: Which file is read last of all?

choices.text: 32MB, because the newest change wins
choices.why: Order of reading decides, not order of time. postgresql.auto.conf is read after every conf.d file.

choices.text: 128MB: postgresql.auto.conf overrides conf.d
choices.why: Right. Until somebody runs ALTER SYSTEM RESET, the emergency value hides the repository's, which is why the rule is to move it into the repo the same day.

choices.text: 32MB, because provision.sh deletes postgresql.auto.conf before reloading
choices.why: The script touches only 50-shop.conf and pg_hba.conf. It knows nothing about postgresql.auto.conf.

choices.text: The reload fails because two files disagree about work_mem
choices.why: Disagreement between files is normal; the later one simply wins.

prompt: Why does provision.sh add one exact line to the end of pg_hba.conf instead of copying a file of its own, as it does for the parameters?
hint: In pg_hba.conf, what does position mean?

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 cannot include files from pg_hba.conf
choices.why: It can; version 16 added include directives there. Ubuntu's file simply does not use them.

choices.text: pg_hba.conf is reloaded separately and must stay one file
choices.why: The same reload rereads both, and one file is not a requirement of the server.

choices.text: Lines appended at the end take priority over earlier ones
choices.why: The opposite: the first line that matches decides. The end is safe only because nothing earlier matches 10.0.0.0/24.

choices.text: Ubuntu's file uses no include, and line order is the meaning
choices.why: Right. The first matching line decides, so a line is placed where nothing above it matches the same connections.

prompt: What does it mean that provision.sh is idempotent?
hint: Run it once, run it again.

choices.text: It restarts the server whenever a parameter requires it
choices.why: It never restarts; it reports RESTART NEEDED and leaves the decision to a person.

choices.text: It undoes everything it did if any step fails
choices.why: set -e stops it at the first failure; nothing is rolled back. That would be a transaction, not idempotence.

choices.text: It runs the same way on any Linux distribution
choices.why: It assumes Ubuntu's paths and apt. Portability is a different property.

choices.text: Running it twice is the same as running it once
choices.why: Right. A second run finds nothing missing and changes nothing, which is what 'nothing to change' reported.

prompt: A first draft of the script appends the pg_hba.conf line with `echo "$HBA" >> "$ETC/pg_hba.conf"` and no check. What happens on the third run?
hint: What did grep -qxF prevent?

choices.text: echo refuses to write a line that already exists in the file
choices.why: echo knows nothing about what a file already holds. Checking is the script's job.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rejects the duplicate on reload and keeps the old file
choices.why: Duplicate lines are legal in pg_hba.conf; the first match decides and the rest are never reached.

choices.text: The file holds the line three times
choices.why: Right. Every run appends it again. The server tolerates the copies, and the file stops describing anything a person meant.

choices.text: set -e stops the script because the line exists
choices.why: Appending succeeds whether or not the line is there, so set -e has nothing to stop.

prompt: The first run ended with `RESTART NEEDED for: listen_addresses, shared_buffers`. Why does the script print this instead of restarting?
hint: What does a restart do to the people connected?

choices.text: A script cannot restart a systemd service
choices.why: It already runs systemctl reload; restart would be one word away. It is a decision, not a limitation.

choices.text: Those two parameters are applied by the next reload
choices.why: They are read only at start; no reload applies them, which is why pending_restart flagged them.

choices.text: Restarting would undo the role and database it just created
choices.why: Roles and databases are in the data directory and survive any restart.

choices.text: A restart drops every connection, so when is a person's call
choices.why: Right. On a fresh machine now is fine; on a busy server it waits for a quiet hour.

prompt: Put the steps of a configuration change, as the lesson made the work_mem change, in order.
hint: The server is the last thing to hear about it.
items: Read the change with git diff
Commit it with the reason in the message
Run provision.sh, which copies the file and reloads
trap: Editing the deployed file first is the drift the lesson is about.

prompt: What is the difference between `pg_settings` and `pg_file_settings`?
hint: One is the server, one is the disk.

choices.text: pg_settings is per database, pg_file_settings is for the whole cluster
choices.why: Both describe the cluster; what separates them is running values against file contents.

choices.text: Running values against what the files say now
choices.why: Right. pg_file_settings rereads the files each time you query it, so it shows lines the server refused.

choices.text: pg_file_settings only lists postgresql.auto.conf
choices.why: It lists every configuration file the server reads, including conf.d; the lesson's query read 50-shop.conf.

choices.text: pg_settings updates only after a restart
choices.why: A reload updates it for every parameter that a reload can change.

prompt: After the hand edit with `log_min_duraton_statement`, `systemctl reload` printed nothing. What did the server do with the correct `work_mem = 64MB` line above the typo?
hint: Read the last line of the log.

choices.text: Applied it, and skipped only the misspelt line
choices.why: The log said 'no changes were applied': a file with an error is refused whole, and SHOW work_mem stayed at 32MB.

choices.text: Applied it after a restart, since work_mem needs one
choices.why: work_mem needs only a reload; the change from 16MB to 32MB took effect without a restart.

choices.text: Nothing: the file was refused whole
choices.why: Right. The server kept running on the previous values; only the log and pg_file_settings said so.

choices.text: Stopped the server until the file is fixed
choices.why: A reload with errors leaves the server running on its old values. The danger is that it looks fine.

prompt: pg_settings showed `shared_buffers` with setting 131072 and unit 8kB. How many megabytes is that?
hint: Multiply, then divide by 1024.

prompt: A server's pg_settings shows `pending_restart = t` for max_connections, and pg_file_settings shows no errors. What has happened?
hint: pending_restart compares the file with what is running.

choices.text: A file was changed and reloaded; the value waits for a start
choices.why: Right. The file is sound and the server read it, but max_connections is taken only at start.

choices.text: The file has a typo that pg_file_settings could not detect
choices.why: A typo would have shown as an error and stopped the reload applying anything, so pending_restart would not have been set.

choices.text: The server crashed and came back with defaults
choices.why: A start reads every file, so after one nothing would be pending.

choices.text: ALTER DATABASE set max_connections for one database
choices.why: max_connections cannot be set per database; it is a property of the whole server.

prompt: Match each tool or object to what it manages.
hint: One logs in, one talks to a provider, one is a file.

pairs.right: A managed service, through the provider's API
One kind of server, from one repository
The parameters of an RDS PostgreSQL

right_distractors: The rows inside the shop database

prompt: A team manages work_mem with Ansible's `community.postgresql.postgresql_set`. An engineer fixes an incident with `ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem`. What happens on Ansible's next run?
hint: Which file does that module manage?

choices.text: It sets its own value back and reports changed
choices.why: Right. The engineer edited the tool's file; a fix that should stay has to go into the playbook.

choices.text: Nothing: Ansible manages conf.d and never sees postgresql.auto.conf
choices.why: postgresql_set works through ALTER SYSTEM itself, so postgresql.auto.conf is exactly the file it manages.

choices.text: Ansible fails, because two writers disagree
choices.why: It reports changed and moves on; a module does not refuse a value it was told to set.

choices.text: The server keeps both, applying the higher one
choices.why: A parameter has one value; there is no rule that prefers the larger.

prompt: On a managed service there is no shell and no conf.d. What does Terraform keep under version control instead?
hint: The service itself, described as resources.

choices.text: A copy of the provider's postgresql.conf
choices.why: The provider never hands you the file; you describe parameters through its API.

choices.text: Its resources, parameters included
choices.why: Right. The instance, its version and a parameter group are resources in files, and terraform plan lists every difference from what the provider reports.

choices.text: A nightly dump of every database
choices.why: Backups are data, not configuration, and db-reliability covers them.

choices.text: The SQL of every ALTER SYSTEM run on the service
choices.why: Terraform describes the end state, not a history of commands.

prompt: A colleague's provisioning script prints `wrote 50-shop.conf` and `reloaded` on every run, including the second. What is the most likely cause?
hint: What makes the comparison fail every time?

choices.text: The server needs a restart that never happens
choices.why: A pending restart would print RESTART NEEDED, not cause the file to be rewritten.

choices.text: Something else rewrites the deployed file between runs
choices.why: Right, or the script writes something that differs each time, such as a date. Either way the second run is the alarm.

choices.text: reload changes the file's owner, so cmp sees a difference
choices.why: cmp compares contents only, and a reload rewrites no file.

choices.text: Idempotent scripts report every step as a reminder
choices.why: An idempotent script reports what it changed, and the lesson's said 'nothing to change' on its second run.

prompt: After running provision.sh on the course server, where `shop` already exists and belongs to `ana`, who owns the database `shop`?
hint: What exactly does the database step check?

choices.text: shop_owner
choices.why: The step only creates the database when the name is missing; it never changes an owner.

choices.text: postgres, because the script runs as postgres
choices.why: Running as postgres does not transfer anything; nothing in the script runs ALTER DATABASE.

choices.text: ana
choices.why: Right. The check asks whether a database called shop exists, and it does. A script checks what it was written to check.

choices.text: Nobody: the script stops with an error because shop exists
choices.why: The check finds shop and skips the step without error.

prompt: The query `SELECT ... FROM pg_file_settings WHERE error IS NOT NULL` returns no rows, yet `SHOW work_mem` disagrees with 50-shop.conf. Where do you look next?
hint: The files are sound. What can override them?

choices.text: The log, for a failed reload
choices.why: A failed reload would show as an error in pg_file_settings, and there is none.

choices.text: Re-run provision.sh until the values agree
choices.why: The script rewrites 50-shop.conf, which is already right; it never touches what overrides it.

choices.text: sourcefile in pg_settings, then \drds
choices.why: Right. A later file such as postgresql.auto.conf, or a setting attached to the database or role, would explain it, and those two show where.

choices.text: Restart the server so it rereads every file
choices.why: A restart reads the same files and the same catalogue, and the value would come back.

prompt: Which of these are drift the settings.sql query against one database can miss? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does a connection to the database ana see?

choices.text: ALTER DATABASE shop SET work_mem
choices.why: Yes. It applies only inside shop.

choices.text: ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout
choices.why: Yes. It applies only to sessions of that role.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem, after a reload
choices.why: That one showed up: work_mem = 64MB was in the diff.

choices.text: A line in a conf.d file, after a reload
choices.why: A reloaded file value is in pg_settings for every database.

prompt: After ALTER SYSTEM has fixed an emergency and the value has been committed to the repository, `ALTER SYSTEM ___ work_mem` removes it from postgresql.auto.conf.
hint: The opposite of SET.
